# The Paths We Make by Walking

On almost every university campus, there is a place where the sidewalk makes a polite right angle and the grass beside it has been worn down to bare dirt along the diagonal. Landscape architects call these "desire lines" or "desire paths": the routes people actually take, as opposed to the ones they were given. I've come to think they are one of the most honest things in the built world.

A paved path is a proposal. Someone sat at a drafting table, or more recently in front of a screen, and decided how people *should* move from the library to the dining hall. Often they had good reasons: symmetry, drainage, a desire to frame a view of the clock tower, a budget that allowed for exactly this much concrete. A desire path is the reply. It says, without malice, *we'd rather go this way.* No committee approved it. No one person made it. It exists because hundreds of individuals, each making a small private decision to save eleven seconds, happened to agree.

There's something beautiful in how that agreement forms. The first person to cut across the lawn is a trespasser. The tenth is following a faint suggestion. By the hundredth, the grass has given up, and walking the diagonal feels less like rebellion than like obeying the obvious. The path teaches its own use. Every footstep is both a vote and an invitation for the next voter. Ant colonies do something similar with pheromone trails, reinforcing the routes that work until the whole colony seems to "know" the shortest way to food, though no single ant knows anything of the kind. We like to think of ourselves as more deliberate than ants, but a muddy shortcut across a quad suggests otherwise, or suggests, at least, that deliberation and swarm behavior aren't as far apart as we assume.

Planners have responded to desire paths in roughly three ways. The first is resistance: fences, hedges, signs that say KEEP OFF THE GRASS, the architectural equivalent of a parent insisting that the child is wrong about what they want. This rarely works for long. People step over low fences. They squeeze through gaps in hedges, creating new desire paths around the obstacles meant to prevent the old ones. The second response is surrender after the fact: someone eventually notices the brown scar in the lawn and paves it, conceding that the walkers were right. The third, and most interesting, is anticipation. There's a story, possibly apocryphal and told about several different campuses, of a designer who refused to lay any sidewalks at all when a new set of buildings opened. He planted grass everywhere, waited a year, and then paved wherever the grass had died.

Whether or not that story happened exactly as told, I love what it represents: a kind of design humility. It admits that the people who will use a space know things the designer can't know in advance. Not because they're smarter, but because they're *there*, carrying heavy bags in the rain, late for class, wanting to stay under the trees on a hot afternoon. Their knowledge is distributed and practical and impossible to gather through a survey, because most of them couldn't articulate it if asked. They can only demonstrate it with their feet.

This tension between the plan and the practice shows up everywhere once you start looking. Software designers watch how users actually click, and discover that the carefully organized menu goes ignored while everyone hunts for the search bar. Languages have grammar books, but the language itself lives in the mouths of speakers, who wear shortcuts into it constantly: "going to" becomes "gonna," "God be with you" becomes "goodbye." Linguists who once saw these changes as corruption now tend to see them the way an enlightened landscape architect sees a dirt trail: as evidence of what people need. Cities themselves are layered records of this. The crooked streets of old European towns often follow ancient footpaths and cow tracks, routes that made sense to someone walking to market a thousand years ago and have been preserved, paved over and over, long after the market vanished.

I don't want to romanticize desire paths too much. Sometimes the planners are right and the crowd is wrong. Some shortcuts erode hillsides, trample fragile plants, or lead people across dangerous roads. The collective wisdom of feet optimizes for one thing, mostly convenience in the moment, and can be blind to everything else. A path that saves eleven seconds for each of ten thousand people might also destroy a meadow that took decades to grow. The swarm doesn't weigh these things; it can't. That's what deliberation is for. The best outcome is probably neither pure top-down design nor pure bottom-up wandering, but a conversation between them: plans that bend to observed behavior, and behavior that is sometimes gently redirected for reasons the individual walker can't see.

Still, I find myself siding with the paths more often than not. There's a lesson in them that extends beyond landscaping, something about the gap between how we think life should be arranged and how it actually gets lived. Many of us carry around internal sidewalks: the tidy routes we've planned for our careers, our habits, our days. And many of us, if we looked honestly, would find worn diagonals cutting across them. The thing we keep doing even though it wasn't in the plan. The friend we keep calling. The hobby that quietly ate the time we'd allotted for something more respectable. It's tempting to see these as failures of discipline, and sometimes they are. But sometimes they're information. Sometimes the trampled grass knows something the blueprint didn't.

The poet Antonio Machado wrote, in lines that have been quoted so often they risk becoming wallpaper, *"Caminante, no hay camino, se hace camino al andar"*: traveler, there is no road; the road is made by walking. It's usually read as inspiration, a call to forge your own way. But I think it's also simply a description. Roads *are* made by walking, whether we intend them or not. Every repeated choice presses down the grass a little further. The question is only whether we notice the paths we're making, and whether, when we finally do, we have the grace to pave them, or the wisdom to let the grass grow back.
